Every tenant reads these; a tenant that saves its own tour under the same slug overrides it for itself only. `narration` + `action_hint` are the PHASE-2 video recording script and are never shown to a user in the app. Anchor syntax: tour:<data-tour-id> | text:<visible text> | css:<selector> | null = centered card (an anchor that does not resolve degrades to a centered card). v2 (2026-08-10): adds the Point of Sale pack (setup wizard, sales tax, the register, stock + activations, who can use it) and the imports/daily-upload walk-through. Where a module is incomplete the step SAYS SO rather than describing a flow that does not work — a training pack that lies is worse than no training pack.

tours.title: Close out your day
tours.description: Count your drawer, log any cash you took out of the envelope, and submit the day's close.

steps.title: Closing out your day
steps.body: This is the form you fill in at the end of every shift. It takes about two minutes. You will enter what you collected, count the drawer, list anything you paid out of the envelope, photograph the envelope, and submit. Click Next and we'll go through it together.
steps.narration: At the end of every shift you close the store out here. It takes about two minutes: enter what you collected, count the drawer, list anything you paid out of the envelope, photograph it, and submit.
steps.action_hint: Open /closing/submit. Hold on the empty form for two seconds.

steps.title: Start with the date, store and your name
steps.body: The date defaults to today and the store to yours. Change the date only if you are closing out for a day you missed. Pick your own name in Employee — the close is filed under whoever is named here.
steps.narration: Start at the top. The date defaults to today and the store to yours. Pick your own name under Employee, because the close is filed under whoever is named here.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the Date, Store and Employee fields. Click the Employee picker and select a rep.

steps.title: Enter what you collected, by payment type
steps.body: Type in the amount for each payment type exactly as it shows on your X-report — cash, card, and any other tender your store uses. If your store doesn't use a tender, leave it at zero.
steps.narration: Now enter what you collected, one line per payment type, exactly as it shows on your X-report. Leave anything your store doesn't use at zero.
steps.action_hint: Type amounts into two or three tender boxes.

steps.title: The total adds itself up
steps.body: This box is calculated for you from the lines above — you cannot type in it. If it doesn't match your X-report total, one of the tender amounts above is wrong.
steps.narration: The total adds itself up from the lines above. If it doesn't match your X-report, a tender amount above is wrong.
steps.action_hint: Point at the calculated total.

steps.title: Bill payments are part of the total, not extra
steps.body: If a customer paid a phone bill, that money is already inside the cash or card figure above. These boxes just tell us how much of it was bill payments — they are never added on top.
steps.narration: Bill payments are already inside the cash or card figures above. These boxes only tell us how much of the money was bill payments. They're never added on top.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the ePay-on-cash / on-credit / on-financing boxes.

steps.title: Count your transactions
steps.body: Enter how many of each kind of transaction you did today. These counts are what your daily targets and your activation numbers are checked against, so take a second to get them right.
steps.narration: Enter how many of each kind of transaction you did. These counts feed your daily targets and activation numbers, so take a second to get them right.
steps.action_hint: Type numbers into two count boxes.

steps.title: Money you took out of the envelope
steps.body: This is the part that is new. Anything paid out of the envelope in cash — a rep's advance, a repair, supplies — goes here as its own line, with a category, an amount and a short description. It is not a free-for-all box: your manager approves each line.
steps.narration: This part is new. Anything you paid out of the envelope in cash goes here as its own line, with a category, an amount and a description. Your manager approves each line.
steps.action_hint: Scroll to the expenses section and pause on the empty state.

steps.title: Add one line per payment
steps.body: Click this for each separate payment. Pick the category first — if you pick a payroll or commission category, the form asks which employee the money went to, because that payment has to land on that person's record. Every line needs an amount and a description.
steps.narration: Click Add expense line for each separate payment. Pick the category first. If it's payroll or commission, the form asks which employee the money went to, so it lands on their record. Every line needs an amount and a description.
steps.action_hint: Click ＋ Add expense line, choose a category, enter an amount, type a description.

steps.title: Photograph the envelope
steps.body: Take a photo of the sealed envelope. The app reads the cash figure off the photo and compares it with what you typed. If they don't match it says so — check the count before you submit rather than after.
steps.narration: Take a photo of the sealed envelope. The app reads the cash figure off the photo and compares it to what you typed, and tells you if they don't match.
steps.action_hint: Click the photo button; show the read-back panel with a matching read.

steps.title: Submit — and what happens next
steps.body: Your close is checked against what the system already knows about the day. If the numbers line up, you're done. If they don't, you'll be asked to recount, and if it still doesn't match, your manager reviews it. That's normal — it protects you as much as the store.
steps.narration: Hit Submit. Your close is checked against what the system already knows about the day. If it doesn't line up you'll be asked to recount, and after that your manager reviews it.
steps.action_hint: Click Submit closing; show the success state and the entry appearing in today's list.

steps.title: That's the whole close
steps.body: Tenders, counts, envelope expenses, photo, submit. The expense lines you entered will show up for your manager to approve, and the cash you took out is already subtracted from what the store has to deposit. You can re-run this walk-through any time from the ? button.
steps.narration: That's the whole close: tenders, counts, envelope expenses, photo, submit. The expenses go to your manager to approve, and the cash you took out is already subtracted from the store's deposit.
steps.action_hint: Fade out on the submitted list.

tours.title: Verify closings and pay from the envelope
tours.description: For DMs: check your stores' closings, approve expense lines, then pay commission, salary and expenses out of the envelope and deposit the rest.

steps.title: Your daily money routine
steps.body: Two pages, in this order. First you verify what your reps submitted and approve their expense lines. Then you pay out what is owed from the envelope and deposit whatever is left. This walk-through covers both.
steps.narration: There are two pages, in this order. First verify what your reps submitted and approve their expense lines. Then pay out what's owed from the envelope and deposit the rest.
steps.action_hint: Open /closing/verify.

steps.title: Everything your stores submitted
steps.body: One block per store, one row per rep. Pick the date at the top. A store with nothing submitted is a store that hasn't closed out — that is the first thing to chase.
steps.narration: This page shows everything your stores submitted: one block per store, one row per rep. A store with nothing submitted hasn't closed out yet — chase that first.
steps.action_hint: Set the date, expand a store block.

steps.title: Approve or reject each expense line
steps.body: Every line the rep entered under envelope expenses shows here with its category, amount and description. Approve the ones you recognise; reject anything you don't. Only approved lines become payable and only approved lines reduce the store's deposit.
steps.narration: Every envelope expense the rep entered shows here. Approve the ones you recognise and reject the ones you don't. Only approved lines become payable and reduce the deposit.
steps.action_hint: Click Approve on one expense line; show the state change.

steps.title: Mark the store verified
steps.body: Once the numbers look right and the expense lines are dealt with, mark the store verified. That is what tells the rest of the system this day is settled for that store.
steps.narration: Once the numbers look right and the expenses are dealt with, mark the store verified. That tells the rest of the system this day is settled.
steps.action_hint: Click Mark verified.

steps.title: Now pay what's owed
steps.body: This page answers one question: how much cash has to come out of the envelope today, and out of which envelopes. Pick the store and the date at the top to load it.
steps.narration: Now to the payout page. It answers one question: how much cash has to come out of the envelope today, and out of which envelopes.
steps.action_hint: Navigate to /closing/envelope-payout, pick a store.

steps.title: What is due, and what you actually have
steps.body: Commission due, salary due and approved expenses due add up to the total cash required. Next to it is the cash actually on hand at this store. If the cash on hand is lower, it turns red — you cannot pay everything today.
steps.narration: Commission, salary and approved expenses add up to the total cash required. Next to it is the cash actually on hand. If it's lower, it turns red and you can't pay everything today.
steps.action_hint: Pan across the five stat tiles.

steps.title: Pay one person, or one expense, at a time
steps.body: Each person and each approved expense is its own line with its own button. You never pay a lump sum — you pay a named amount to a named person, so every dollar has a record.
steps.narration: Each person and each approved expense is its own line with its own button. You never pay a lump sum — you pay a named amount to a named person.
steps.action_hint: Click Pay from envelope on a commission line.

steps.title: The app picks the fewest envelopes
steps.body: It works out the smallest number of envelopes that cover this exact amount, and shows you each one: the date and rep it belongs to, what's in it, how much to take, and what will be left. Open only those envelopes.
steps.narration: The app works out the fewest envelopes that cover this exact amount, and shows each one: what's in it, how much to take, and what's left. Open only those envelopes.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the plan table so each column is readable.

steps.title: Confirm once the cash is physically counted out
steps.body: Press this only after you have actually taken the cash. It records the withdrawal against each envelope and marks the person paid or the expense settled in one go — you do not have to write it down anywhere else.
steps.narration: Press Confirm only after you've actually taken the cash. It records the withdrawal against each envelope and marks the payment settled in one go.
steps.action_hint: Click Confirm; show the line disappearing from what's due.

steps.title: Deposit what's left
steps.body: This figure is the cash still in the store after everything you just paid out. It updates itself as you confirm each payout. That number, and only that number, is what goes to the bank.
steps.narration: This figure is the cash still in the store after everything you just paid. It updates as you confirm each payout, and it's what goes to the bank.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the deposit figure updating.

steps.title: That's the routine
steps.body: Verify, approve expenses, pay from the envelope, deposit the remainder. Do it in that order every day and the store's cash position stays correct without anyone reconciling it by hand.
steps.narration: Verify, approve expenses, pay from the envelope, deposit the remainder. In that order, every day, and the cash position stays correct on its own.
steps.action_hint: Fade out.

tours.title: Where your commission comes from
tours.description: How the monthly commission is produced, and how the new Daily Commission page shows what a rep has earned so far and what they have already been advanced in cash.

steps.title: Two different numbers, two different pages
steps.body: Commission has a monthly number and a daily number and they are not the same thing. The monthly number is what actually gets paid. The daily number is an early estimate so nobody is guessing mid-month. We'll look at both.
steps.narration: Commission has a monthly number and a daily number, and they're not the same. The monthly number is what gets paid. The daily number is an early estimate so nobody's guessing mid-month.
steps.action_hint: Open /commcalc.

steps.title: The monthly picture
steps.body: This dashboard is the month you are looking at, the reps in it, and whether the month has been calculated yet. The line under the title tells you the state: not calculated, running, or done.
steps.narration: This dashboard shows the month you're looking at, the reps in it, and whether the month has been calculated yet.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the header and the calculation status line.

steps.title: Running the month
steps.body: This re-runs the whole month from the sales and payout data. It is safe to re-run — it restates the month, it doesn't add to it. It can take a while on a big month, so start it once and let it finish rather than clicking again.
steps.narration: This re-runs the whole month from the sales and payout data. It restates the month rather than adding to it, and it can take a while — start it once and let it finish.
steps.action_hint: Hover the Run Calculation button. Do not click during recording.

steps.target: text:What this calculation did not pay
steps.title: What it deliberately did NOT pay
steps.body: When a calculation skips something on purpose — a device category that doesn't qualify, an activation it couldn't classify — it says so here instead of quietly paying zero. If a rep says their commission looks light, read this box first.
steps.narration: When the calculation skips something on purpose it says so here instead of quietly paying zero. If a rep says their commission looks light, read this box first.
steps.action_hint: Show the notices panel on a month that has one.

steps.title: The daily view
steps.body: This page is new. It shows what each rep has probably earned so far this period, based on the sales that have landed. Read the line under the title carefully: this is an expected figure, not a payslip.
steps.narration: This page is new. It shows what each rep has probably earned so far, based on the sales that have landed. It's an expected figure, not a payslip.
steps.action_hint: Navigate to /commcalc/daily-commission.

steps.title: Accrued, advanced, and the balance
steps.body: Accrued is what they look to have earned. Paid in cash is what has already been handed to them out of an envelope. Unpaid balance is the difference — roughly what is still coming to them. Over-advanced flags anyone who has taken more than they've earned so far.
steps.narration: Accrued is what they look to have earned. Paid in cash is what's already been handed to them from an envelope. Unpaid balance is the difference, and Over-advanced flags anyone who's taken more than they've earned.
steps.action_hint: Pan across the tiles, ending on Over-advanced.

steps.title: Recording cash you handed over
steps.body: If you give a rep cash against their commission, record it here — or, better, pay it through the Envelope Payout page, which records it for you. Either way it changes the paid figure only. It never reduces what the rep is actually owed at month end.
steps.narration: If you hand a rep cash against their commission, record it here — or pay it through the Envelope Payout page, which records it for you. Either way it never reduces what they're owed at month end.
steps.action_hint: Show the advance form; fill it without submitting.

steps.title: When a day's sales arrive late
steps.body: The daily figure updates itself every day once the sales feed lands. Use this only when a day's sales came in late and that day still looks empty. Re-running a date restates it — it never doubles it, and it never touches anyone's actual pay.
steps.narration: The daily figure updates itself once the sales feed lands. Use this only when a day's sales came in late. Re-running a date restates it — it never doubles it and never touches actual pay.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the date box and the Recompute button.

steps.title: The rule to remember
steps.body: Daily is an estimate that helps you manage the month. Monthly is the number that pays. Cash advances move between them; they never change the total a rep earns.
steps.narration: Daily is an estimate that helps you manage the month. Monthly is the number that pays. Cash advances move between them and never change what a rep earns.
steps.action_hint: Fade out.

tours.title: Time clock and schedules
tours.description: Read the clock-in punches with their selfie, GPS and face check, then build next week's schedule from last week or a saved template.

steps.title: Hours in, schedule out
steps.body: Two pages sit behind payroll: Time Clock, which is what actually happened, and Schedule, which is what you planned. This walk-through shows how to read the first and build the second.
steps.narration: Two pages sit behind payroll: Time Clock, what actually happened, and Schedule, what you planned.
steps.action_hint: Open /storeops/timeclock.

steps.title: Every punch, with proof
steps.body: Reps clock in and out from the mobile portal, not from here. This page is the record: who, when, which store, and the selfie, GPS and face check taken at the moment they punched.
steps.narration: Reps clock in from the mobile portal. This page is the record: who, when, which store, and the selfie, GPS and face check taken at the moment they punched.
steps.action_hint: Show the punch table with a few rows.

steps.title: Filter to what you're actually reviewing
steps.body: Set the date range, then narrow by store, market or person. Everything below — the punch count, the total hours and the export — follows whatever you pick here.
steps.narration: Set the date range, then narrow by store, market or person. The punch count, the hours total and the export all follow the filter.
steps.action_hint: Change the date range, pick one store.

steps.title: Hours, and the lunch deduction
steps.body: The badges give you the punch count and total hours for the filter. Where an automatic lunch has been taken off, the row shows the deduction and the net hours underneath — so a rep asking why their hours look short can be answered from this screen.
steps.narration: The badges give you punch count and total hours. Where an automatic lunch has been deducted, the row shows the deduction and the net hours, so you can answer a rep on the spot.
steps.action_hint: Zoom on a row with a lunch deduction.

steps.title: That lunch rule is yours to set
steps.body: The automatic lunch is a setting, not a hard rule — how long a shift has to be before it applies, and how much comes off. Change it here and it applies going forward.
steps.narration: The automatic lunch is a setting: how long a shift has to be before it applies, and how much comes off. Change it here and it applies going forward.
steps.action_hint: Open the Lunch Break Settings panel, then close it.

steps.title: Two ways to look at a week
steps.body: By store shows one store's whole week, which is how you spot an uncovered day. By employee shows one person across every store, which is how you spot someone doubled up or short of hours.
steps.narration: By store shows one store's whole week — that's how you spot an uncovered day. By employee shows one person across every store, which is how you spot someone doubled up.
steps.action_hint: Navigate to /storeops/schedule, toggle between the two views.

steps.title: Don't build a week from scratch
steps.body: Most weeks look like the last one. Copy last week pulls those shifts forward so you only fix the exceptions. Copy weeks pushes this week's pattern into several weeks ahead in one go.
steps.narration: Most weeks look like the last one. Copy last week pulls those shifts forward so you only fix the exceptions, and Copy weeks pushes this week's pattern several weeks ahead.
steps.action_hint: Click Copy last week; show the grid filling.

steps.title: Save the pattern once
steps.body: If a week is the shape you want to repeat, save it as the template. From then on Apply template fills any empty week with that pattern in one click.
steps.narration: If a week is the shape you want to repeat, save it as the template. Apply template then fills any empty week with that pattern in one click.
steps.action_hint: Click Save template, move to a new week, click Apply template.

steps.title: Why it matters downstream
steps.body: The schedule isn't just a rota. It decides who is expected in which store, which is what the closing checks, the time-off approvals and the payroll hours all measure against. A wrong schedule shows up as a wrong number somewhere else.
steps.narration: The schedule isn't just a rota. It decides who's expected in which store, and the closing checks, time-off approvals and payroll hours all measure against it.
steps.action_hint: Fade out on the filled week.

tours.title: Store expenses and the P&L
tours.description: Enter each store's monthly running costs, and see how they land on the profit and loss statement.

steps.title: What a store costs to run
steps.body: Rent, wages, utilities, everything else — entered once a month per store. It's a small job that decides whether the profit figure for that store means anything, so it's worth doing properly.
steps.narration: Rent, wages, utilities, everything else — entered once a month per store. It's a small job that decides whether the store's profit figure means anything.
steps.action_hint: Open /commcalc/expenses.

steps.title: One month, one grid
steps.body: Pick the month at the top. Each column is a store, each row is an expense line. You are filling in a grid, not a form per store.
steps.narration: Pick the month at the top. Each column is a store, each row is an expense line. You're filling in a grid, not a form per store.
steps.action_hint: Set the month; show the grid.

steps.title: Add the lines your business actually has
steps.body: The expense lines are yours to define — add whatever your business really spends money on. They are not fixed by us, and once added a line stays available for every store and every month.
steps.narration: The expense lines are yours to define. Add whatever your business actually spends money on — once added, the line stays available for every store and every month.
steps.action_hint: Click Add expense, name a line.

steps.title: Let payroll fill itself in
steps.body: Rather than typing wages in by hand, pull them from the hours already recorded on the time clock. Same for commission. Both are still editable afterwards if you need to override a figure.
steps.narration: Rather than typing wages in by hand, pull them from the hours already on the time clock. Same for commission. Both stay editable if you need to override.
steps.action_hint: Click the fill-salaries button; show the column populating.

steps.title: Or do a whole month in a spreadsheet
steps.body: Download the template, fill it in offline, upload it back. Useful when a bookkeeper does the month in one sitting instead of you typing it store by store.
steps.narration: You can also download the template, fill it in offline and upload it back — useful when a bookkeeper does the whole month in one sitting.
steps.action_hint: Hover the Template and upload controls.

steps.title: Nothing counts until you save
steps.body: Edits sit on screen until you press Save All. Get in the habit of saving before you change the month, or you'll lose the lot.
steps.narration: Edits sit on screen until you press Save All. Save before you change the month, or you'll lose them.
steps.action_hint: Click Save All; show the confirmation.

steps.title: Where those numbers end up
steps.body: The profit and loss statement takes the income the system already knows about, subtracts cost of goods, then subtracts the expenses you just entered. Pick the period and the company at the top.
steps.narration: The profit and loss takes the income the system already knows, subtracts cost of goods, then subtracts the expenses you just entered.
steps.action_hint: Navigate to /accounts/pl, set the period.

steps.title: Reading it honestly
steps.body: A store showing an unusually good profit is usually a store whose expenses haven't been entered for that month — not a star performer. When a number looks too good, check the expense grid before you celebrate.
steps.narration: A store showing an unusually good profit is usually a store whose expenses weren't entered — not a star performer. When a number looks too good, check the expense grid first.
steps.action_hint: Compare two stores; fade out.

tours.title: Asset charges and where the losses are
tours.description: Read the charges dashboard: what is being billed to you, what has been denied, and which of it is a real loss you can still act on.

steps.title: The money side of inventory
steps.body: Phones that came in on financing carry charges: fees, balances, denied appeals, returns that were never reimbursed. This dashboard puts all of it on one screen so nothing quietly ages out.
steps.narration: Phones that came in on financing carry charges: fees, balances, denied appeals, returns that were never reimbursed. This dashboard puts all of it on one screen.
steps.action_hint: Open /commcalc/asset/dashboard.

steps.title: Set the window first
steps.body: All time, a month, or a single billing week — then narrow to a market or a store. Every figure below reacts to this bar, so set it before you read any number.
steps.narration: Choose all time, a month, or a single billing week, then narrow to a market or store. Every figure below reacts to this bar.
steps.action_hint: Switch between All time and Month; pick a market.

steps.title: The headline is real money lost
steps.body: This is not a balance owed — it's money already gone: appeals that were denied plus the net loss on returns. Treat it as the number to drive down, and the two figures under it tell you which half to work on.
steps.narration: This headline isn't a balance owed — it's money already gone: denied appeals plus the net loss on returns. The two figures under it tell you which half to work on.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the Total Loss card.

steps.title: Each tile opens the detail behind it
steps.body: The tiles group the charges by what they are — fees, balances, appeals, oddities, returns. Each one shows a total and a count and opens the item-by-item report. The appeals tile is the urgent one: those have deadlines.
steps.narration: The tiles group charges by what they are, each with a total, a count, and a link to the item-by-item report. The appeals tile is the urgent one — those have deadlines.
steps.action_hint: Hover each tile; click into the appeals report and come back.

steps.title: Push the urgent ones to the stores
steps.body: This turns the appeals and unreturned-device problems into flags on the stores that own them, so the people who can actually fix a device get told instead of the list sitting here. Denied appeals go out as critical.
steps.narration: This turns appeals and unreturned devices into flags on the stores that own them, so the people who can fix a device get told instead of the list sitting here.
steps.action_hint: Click Push Flags; show the confirmation.

steps.title: Make it a weekly habit
steps.body: Filter to last week, read the total loss, open appeals, push the flags. Ten minutes a week is the difference between a charge you can still appeal and one you have simply paid.
steps.narration: Filter to last week, read the total loss, open appeals, push the flags. Ten minutes a week is the difference between a charge you can still appeal and one you've simply paid.
steps.action_hint: Fade out on the dashboard.

tours.title: Set up the Point of Sale
tours.description: The 17-step setup that has to be done once per company before anyone rings a sale. Eight steps are required; the rest can wait.

steps.title: Setup is measured, not ticked off
steps.body: This page does not ask you to confirm anything. It looks at your actual data and works out what is still missing — so a step goes green when the thing genuinely exists, and goes back to red if someone later deletes it. You cannot accidentally mark yourself finished.
steps.narration: This page doesn't ask you to confirm anything. It looks at your real data and works out what is still missing, so a step only goes green when the thing genuinely exists.
steps.action_hint: Open /pos/onboarding on a tenant with setup outstanding.

steps.target: text:Set up your Point of Sale
steps.title: Eight of the seventeen are required
steps.body: Required steps are the ones a register cannot work without: your stores, your staff, a carrier, departments, categories, products, sales tax and rate plans. Everything else — vendors, customers, stock, receipt wording — is offered, never enforced. You can open the register with the first eight done.
steps.narration: Eight steps are required — stores, staff, carrier, departments, categories, products, sales tax and plans. The rest are offered, never enforced.
steps.action_hint: Point at the header, then scroll the step list.

steps.title: Red means the register will misbehave
steps.body: A REQUIRED step that is not done is not a formality. Skip products and there is nothing to ring up; skip plans and an activation records no monthly fee, which quietly breaks the commission figures further down the line.
steps.narration: A required step that isn't done isn't a formality — skip plans, for instance, and activations record no monthly fee, which quietly breaks commissions later.
steps.action_hint: Hover a REQUIRED badge.

steps.title: Every step says why it exists
steps.body: Open a step and it tells you what the thing is for, in plain terms, and gives you the button that takes you to the screen where you do it. You are never left guessing which page a step means.
steps.narration: Open a step and it tells you what the thing is for and takes you to the screen where you do it.
steps.action_hint: Expand one step to show the explanation and its link.

steps.title: Re-check after you have been away
steps.body: Do the work on the other screen, come back, press Re-check. The page re-reads your data and the step turns green on its own. If it stays red, the thing you created is not where the step is looking — read the grey reason line, it names the count it found.
steps.narration: Do the work, come back, press Re-check. If a step stays red, the grey reason line tells you the count it actually found.
steps.action_hint: Press Re-check and show a step flipping to DONE.

steps.title: Skip is honest, not a shortcut
steps.body: A few steps cannot be measured from data — deciding who may use POS, whether POS feeds your commissions. Those you acknowledge or skip yourself. A skipped step stays visible and stays skipped until you un-skip it, so nothing disappears just because you were busy.
steps.narration: A few steps can't be measured from data, so you acknowledge or skip them yourself. A skipped step stays visible until you un-skip it.
steps.action_hint: Show Skip for now and Un-skip on the same step.

steps.title: Your stores and staff are already here
steps.body: The first three steps — stores, staff, carrier — are almost always green the moment you arrive. POS reads the same store list and the same employee roster the rest of MetricsPro uses. You are not setting up a second company.
steps.narration: The first three steps are usually already green: POS reads the same stores and the same staff roster the rest of MetricsPro uses.
steps.action_hint: Point at the three Your business steps.

steps.title: Sales tax is the step people get wrong
steps.body: Adding one tax rate turns the step green, and that is NOT the same as being finished. A rate belongs to a store, a market, or the whole company — and any store none of them reaches charges no tax at all. Do this one on the POS Settings screen, where the red banner counts the stores still uncovered, and do not trust a green tick here on its own.
steps.narration: Adding one tax rate turns this step green, and that is not the same as being finished. Check the red coverage banner on POS Settings before you believe it.
steps.action_hint: Point at the Sales tax step, then open /pos/settings in a second tab.

steps.title: The reminder follows you, it does not trap you
steps.body: While a required step is outstanding, a yellow strip sits on every POS page. “Continue later” silences it for this browser session and lets you into the register — you will be asked again next time you sign in. Nothing about the register is locked.
steps.narration: While something required is outstanding, a yellow strip sits on every POS page. Continue later silences it for this session; nothing is locked.
steps.action_hint: Press Continue later, land on the register, show the strip.

tours.title: Sales tax — get every store covered
tours.description: The highest-stakes screen in POS. A store with no rate charges nothing, and you cannot fix that after the customer has left.

steps.title: Why this screen matters more than the others
steps.body: The register does not work tax out for itself. It charges the rate this screen resolves for the store the sale is rung at. If no rate reaches that store, the sale goes through at zero tax, the customer leaves, and the money is yours to find.
steps.narration: The register doesn't work tax out for itself — it charges the rate this screen resolves. If no rate reaches a store, the sale goes through at zero tax and the money is yours to find.
steps.action_hint: Open /pos/settings and scroll to Sales Tax.

steps.title: Three levels, most specific wins
steps.body: A rate can cover one store, a whole market, or the company. The register looks for the store's own rate first, then its market's, then the company default — and stops at the first one it finds. That order is fixed and is the same everywhere, so two screens can never disagree about what a store charges.
steps.narration: A rate can cover one store, a whole market, or the company. The register takes the store's own rate first, then its market's, then the company default.
steps.action_hint: Point at the Sales Tax section header.

steps.title: Read the red banner before anything else
steps.body: If any store has no rate that reaches it, a red banner at the top of this section says how many and names them. That count is the only number on this screen worth acting on immediately. When it is gone you get a green line instead.
steps.narration: If any store has no rate reaching it, a red banner says how many and names them. That's the number to act on first.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the coverage banner.

steps.title: Adding a rate: pick who it applies to
steps.body: Give the rate a name and a percent, then choose what it applies to. “Specific store(s)” lets you tick several at once — the same rate goes on all of them. “A whole market” writes one rate for every store in that market, so changing it later is one edit rather than twenty. “Every store” is the company safety net.
steps.narration: Name the rate, set the percent, then choose whether it applies to specific stores, a whole market, or every store.
steps.action_hint: Open Add Tax Code and switch the Applies-to dropdown through all three.

steps.title: The quickest way to fix a gap
steps.body: Inside the store picker there is a button that selects exactly the stores with no rate. Tick it, type the percent once, save. If they genuinely share a rate, the banner at the top will be gone when the screen reloads.
steps.narration: The store picker has a button that selects exactly the stores with no rate — tick it, type the percent once, save.
steps.action_hint: Press the “only the N with no rate” button, then Save.

steps.title: Or work down the list
steps.body: This opens every store you have, with three columns worth reading together: what is set on the store itself, what it actually charges once markets and the company default are taken into account, and which of the three that came from. Type into any row and press Save rates. A store that already has a rate is updated, never duplicated.
steps.narration: This opens every store with what is set on it, what it actually charges, and where that came from. Type into any row and save.
steps.action_hint: Open the store list and type a rate into two rows.

steps.title: Turning a rate off has consequences downhill
steps.body: Deactivating does not delete — the rate stops applying and the register falls to the next level down. If there is no next level, that store charges nothing. The confirmation box spells out which stores are affected before you agree.
steps.narration: Deactivating stops a rate applying and the register falls to the next level down. If there isn't one, that store charges nothing.
steps.action_hint: Press Deactivate and read the confirmation aloud, then cancel.

steps.title: One thing to know about the setup wizard
steps.body: The POS setup wizard's sales-tax step used to go green as soon as ONE rate existed anywhere in the company — which is how a company with twenty stores and one rate saw a green tick. It now measures every store. Either way, the red banner on THIS screen is the answer you should trust.
steps.narration: The setup wizard's tax step used to go green as soon as one rate existed anywhere. Trust the red banner on this screen.
steps.action_hint: Centered card; no anchor.

tours.title: Ring a sale on the register
tours.description: Open the drawer, build the cart, take payment, print the receipt — and what to do when the register refuses.

steps.title: This is the register
steps.body: Cart on one side, product search on the other, totals bottom right. Everything you need for a walk-in sale is on this one screen — you should not have to leave it once the customer is in front of you.
steps.narration: Cart on one side, product search on the other, totals bottom right. Everything for a walk-in sale is on this one screen.
steps.action_hint: Open /pos/sales.

steps.title: Pick your store first — everything follows from it
steps.body: The store decides which stock you can sell, which tax rate is charged, and which store the sale is booked against. Get it wrong and the sale lands at another door. If your login only covers one store, it is already chosen for you.
steps.narration: The store decides which stock you can sell, which tax you charge, and where the sale is booked. Get it wrong and it lands at another door.
steps.action_hint: Open the store dropdown and choose one.

steps.title: The sale is stamped with YOU
steps.body: Whoever is signed in gets the sale — it is taken from your login, never typed in, so nobody can ring a sale under someone else's name. If the register tells you your login is not linked to an employee record, that is an admin fix in Roles & Access, not something you can work around.
steps.narration: The sale is stamped with whoever is signed in — taken from your login, never typed. If it says your login isn't linked to an employee record, an admin has to set that.
steps.action_hint: Point at the User label in the header.

steps.title: Cash sales may need the drawer open first
steps.body: If your company has turned this on, you must open the register with a float count before a cash transaction is accepted — the same discipline as counting a till at the start of a shift. Card sales are unaffected. If cash is being refused, this is usually why.
steps.narration: If your company requires it, you must open the register with a float count before cash is accepted. If cash is being refused, this is usually why.
steps.action_hint: Show the drawer panel and the opening float.

steps.title: Build the cart
steps.body: Scan a barcode into the box, or search by name and click. Quantities and line discounts are edited on the cart line itself. If a discount box will not accept anything, discounts are switched off for your company in POS Settings — the field says so when you hover it.
steps.narration: Scan a barcode or search by name. Quantities and discounts are edited on the cart line itself.
steps.action_hint: Scan one item, then search another by name.

steps.title: Phones need their serial or IMEI
steps.body: Anything tracked by serial asks for the number before it can leave the cart. That is what ties the handset to this ticket — it is how the device is later matched to an activation, a return, or a chargeback. Do not guess it; scan it.
steps.narration: Anything tracked by serial asks for the number. That's what ties the handset to this ticket for activations, returns and chargebacks later.
steps.action_hint: Add a serialised product and show the serial prompt.

steps.title: Check the total before you take money
steps.body: Subtotal, discounts, tax, total. The tax line is not typed by you — it is the rate your company set for this store. If it reads zero on a taxable sale, stop and tell a manager: that is a setup problem, and it cannot be corrected after the customer has gone.
steps.narration: The tax line isn't typed by you — it's the rate set for this store. If it reads zero on a taxable sale, stop and tell a manager.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the totals block, especially the tax line.

steps.title: Take the payment
steps.body: Choose the method. For cash, type what the customer handed you and the register works out the change — the quick-amount buttons cover the usual notes. Split payments are added one line at a time until the balance is nil.
steps.narration: Choose the method. For cash, type what the customer handed over and the register works out the change. Split payments go on one line at a time.
steps.action_hint: Take a cash payment and show the change calculation.

steps.title: Named sale or quick sale
steps.body: A quick sale needs no customer record and is right for a walk-in accessory. Attach a customer when the sale has a life after today — an activation, a device on a plan, anything you may have to look up later by the person rather than the ticket.
steps.narration: A quick sale needs no customer and suits a walk-in accessory. Attach a customer when the sale has a life after today.
steps.action_hint: Toggle between Quick Sale and Customer Sale.

steps.title: Finding a sale afterwards
steps.body: The Sale Log searches by ticket number, date range, store or customer, and reprints a receipt. Voiding a completed sale is a separate right your manager grants — if the button is not there, that is why, and it is deliberate.
steps.narration: The Sale Log searches by ticket, date, store or customer and reprints receipts. Voiding needs a permission your manager grants.
steps.action_hint: Open the Sale Log and search a date range.

tours.title: Stock, transfers and activations
tours.description: What is on your shelf, moving a unit between stores, and recording an activation with the right dealer code — including the parts that are not finished yet.

steps.title: Two kinds of stock
steps.body: Serialised units — phones, anything with an IMEI — are tracked one at a time, each with its own history. Everything else is a count per store. The tabs on this page separate the two because they behave differently: you can transfer a specific handset, you can only move a quantity of cases.
steps.narration: Serialised units like phones are tracked one at a time. Everything else is a count per store. The tabs separate them because they behave differently.
steps.action_hint: Open /pos/inventory and switch tabs.

steps.title: Filter to the store you are asking about
steps.body: Stock questions are always about one store. Set the store filter first; the status filter then tells you what is available, what is reserved and what has already gone.
steps.narration: Stock questions are always about one store. Set the store filter first, then the status filter.
steps.action_hint: Set the store filter, then the status filter.

steps.title: ⚠️ Known problem — scoped users may see an empty list
steps.body: The stock now in POS was loaded from your existing MetricsPro inventory, and it recorded each unit against a street address rather than the short store code the rest of the system uses. A company-wide login sees everything, so this is easy to miss — but a store or market-scoped manager can see nothing at all. If your list is empty and you know the stock is there, this is why. It is a known fault, not something you have done.
steps.narration: The stock was loaded against street addresses rather than store codes. A company-wide login sees everything, but a store-scoped manager may see nothing. Known fault.
steps.action_hint: Centered card. Compare an admin view with a store-scoped view.

steps.title: Moving a unit between stores
steps.body: A transfer is deliberately three moves, not one: create it, ship it, receive it. The unit belongs to neither store while it is in transit, which is what stops a handset appearing on two shelves at once. Cancel is available until it has been received.
steps.narration: A transfer is three moves — create, ship, receive. The unit belongs to neither store in transit, which stops it appearing on two shelves at once.
steps.action_hint: Walk a transfer from create to receive.

steps.title: Recording an activation
steps.body: An activation hangs off a sale and adds what the carrier needs: the line, the plan, the device and the dealer code. The plan matters beyond paperwork — it carries the monthly fee that your commission figures are worked out from.
steps.narration: An activation adds what the carrier needs: line, plan, device and dealer code. The plan carries the monthly fee your commissions are worked out from.
steps.action_hint: Open /pos/activations and start a new one.

steps.title: The dealer code is how the carrier knows the door
steps.body: A wrong or missing dealer code is the usual reason an activation is never paid. The list here comes from POS Settings, and each code should be attached to the store it belongs to — a code left on “all stores” can be picked at any door, which is exactly how they get mixed up.
steps.narration: A wrong or missing dealer code is the usual reason an activation is never paid. Each code should be attached to the store it belongs to.
steps.action_hint: Open the Dealer Code dropdown.

steps.title: Pull the codes out of your carrier reports
steps.body: You do not have to type these. “Pull from reports” reads the codes out of the carrier data MetricsPro already holds — it shows you what it found before it writes anything, and it only ever adds codes that are missing, so a code you have corrected by hand is never overwritten. A carrier nobody has mapped yet is reported as unmapped rather than guessed at.
steps.narration: Pull from reports reads the codes out of your existing carrier data, shows you what it found before writing, and only adds what's missing.
steps.action_hint: Press Pull from reports and read the preview.

steps.title: What is not finished here yet
steps.body: Purchase orders and receiving against a PO exist but have had little real use. Trade-in credit records the value but does not yet feed the P&L. Treat the activation record as the reliable part and reconcile the money against the carrier's own report, not against this screen.
steps.narration: Purchase orders and trade-in credit are early. Treat the activation record as the reliable part and reconcile money against the carrier's own report.
steps.action_hint: Centered card; no anchor.

tours.title: Give your team access to POS
tours.description: Point of Sale is switched off for every role until you switch it on. This is the five-minute job that makes it appear in the menu for your staff.

steps.title: Nobody can see POS until you turn it on
steps.body: POS arrived after your roles were created, and a role only carries the modules it was given when it was made. So the Point of Sale menu is hidden from everyone except a super-admin — not because anything is broken, but because no role has been granted it yet. This is the screen where that changes.
steps.narration: POS arrived after your roles were created, so no role carries it yet and the menu is hidden from everyone but a super-admin. This is where you change that.
steps.action_hint: Open /admin/roles.

steps.title: Tick Point of Sale on each role that needs it
steps.body: Every role has a Modules list. Tick “Point of Sale” for the roles that should have a register — usually your reps, store managers and admins — and press Save on that role. The menu appears for those people the next time they load the app.
steps.narration: Every role has a Modules list. Tick Point of Sale for the roles that need a register and press Save on that role.
steps.action_hint: Tick Point of Sale on the store manager role and save.

steps.title: A role scoped to “own data” sees no POS at all
steps.body: This one catches people out. Every POS screen needs at least store-level reach — a role set to “only their own data” will have the module ticked and still see nothing. If you want a rep on the register, their role has to be their store, their market, or company-wide.
steps.narration: Every POS screen needs at least store-level reach. A role set to only their own data will have the module ticked and still see nothing.
steps.action_hint: Show the Scope selector and the four options.

steps.title: The four rights inside POS
steps.body: Beyond seeing the module, four things are granted separately: revealing a customer's full identity details, voiding a completed sale, adjusting or receiving stock, and changing POS settings such as tax rates. A rep normally has none of them. Grant them one at a time to the people who genuinely need them.
steps.narration: Four things are granted separately inside POS: revealing customer identity details, voiding a sale, adjusting stock, and changing POS settings such as tax rates.
steps.action_hint: Point at the per-function grants.

steps.title: Link each person to their employee record
steps.body: The register stamps every sale with the signed-in person's employee record. A login with no Employee ID cannot complete a sale at all — it is refused with a message saying exactly that. Set the Employee ID on each user here before their first shift, not during it.
steps.narration: The register stamps every sale with the signed-in person's employee record. A login with no Employee ID cannot complete a sale.
steps.action_hint: Open a user and show the Employee ID field.

steps.title: If you administer more than one company
steps.body: A super-admin can set another company's POS up without being a member of it — pick the company in the switcher and carry on. Everyone else only ever sees and edits their own company's POS, and that boundary is enforced on the server, not just in the menu.
steps.narration: A super-admin can set another company's POS up without being a member of it. Everyone else only ever sees their own company's POS.
steps.action_hint: Show the tenant switcher.

tours.title: Imports: what pulls itself, and what you owe daily
tours.description: The connectors board after the 2026-08-09 changes — why some reports vanished from your list, what 'overdue' really counts, and who is supposed to upload what.

steps.title: One row per report your company needs
steps.body: Each row is a report MetricsPro expects: where it comes from, whether it pulls itself, when it last arrived. This board is the honest picture of what your numbers are actually built from.
steps.narration: Each row is a report MetricsPro expects: where it comes from, whether it pulls itself, and when it last arrived.
steps.action_hint: Open /commcalc/connectors.

steps.title: You only see your own carrier's reports
steps.body: Reports are filtered to the carriers your company actually sells. A Total dealer no longer sees Boost's ePay reports sitting there looking overdue. Reports that belong to no carrier — closing, inventory, distributor invoices — are shown to everyone, because they are not a carrier concept. If a report you need is missing, the fix is to attach the carrier, not to hunt for the report.
steps.narration: Reports are filtered to the carriers you actually sell. Reports that belong to no carrier are shown to everyone.
steps.action_hint: Centered card; mention the Carriers page.

steps.title: Automatic and manual are different promises
steps.body: A report marked automatic is pulled for you on a schedule. Untick automatic and the report stops being chased — it also stops being counted as overdue, which is the point: a report you have decided to upload by hand should not nag you as a failure.
steps.narration: A report marked automatic is pulled on a schedule. Untick it and the report stops being chased and stops counting as overdue.
steps.action_hint: Toggle the automatic tick on one row.

steps.title: Overdue and never-arrived are both real
steps.body: The counts at the top are worth taking seriously — each one has been checked and each is a genuine gap, not noise. “Never” usually means a report nobody has ever uploaded; “overdue” means one that used to arrive and has stopped. Work the never list first: it is usually a credential or a missing decision.
steps.narration: Overdue means a report that used to arrive and has stopped. Never means one nobody has ever uploaded. Work the never list first.
steps.action_hint: Point at the overdue and never counts.

steps.title: Reports that must be uploaded every day need an owner
steps.body: Some reports have to be pulled from a portal by a person, daily. Those carry an owner — the one person who gets told what to upload, for exactly which dates, with the steps to get it. When an automatic pull fails, the same person is told, because a failed robot is still somebody's job.
steps.narration: Some reports must be pulled from a portal daily. Those carry an owner who is told what to upload and for which dates — including when an automatic pull fails.
steps.action_hint: Centered card.

steps.title: ⚠️ Assigning that owner is not on screen yet
steps.body: The daily-upload duty exists and is already working out what is owed, but the screen for naming the person has not been built. Until it is, an unassigned duty shows up as a warning in the admin attention panel — “Daily upload has no owner” — and an administrator has to set the owner for you. Do not read the warning as a data problem; it is a missing screen.
steps.narration: The daily-upload duty works, but the screen for naming the person hasn't been built. Until then an unassigned duty shows as a warning in the admin panel.
steps.action_hint: Show the Daily upload has no owner warning in the attention panel.

steps.title: When an import fails, it is written down
steps.body: Failures are logged rather than shown once and lost. If a file went in and the numbers did not move, look here before re-uploading — a second upload of the same file is recognised and skipped, so repeating it will not tell you anything new.
steps.narration: Failures are logged rather than shown once and lost. Look here before re-uploading — a repeat of the same file is recognised and skipped.
steps.action_hint: Open /failures and filter to import errors.

tours.title: Clocking out — and when you need permission
tours.description: Always clock out when you leave. What happens if you forget, and when working late or coming back for a second session needs your manager's OK.

steps.title: Clocking out the right way
steps.body: This is your clock-in / clock-out screen. The most important habit is simple: clock out yourself every time you leave. This walk-through shows you exactly how, and explains what the system now does if you forget or if you work past your shift. Click Next and we'll go through it.
steps.narration: This is your clock screen. The one habit that matters most: clock out yourself every time you leave. Let's walk through how, and what happens if you forget or work late.
steps.action_hint: Open /portal while clocked in, so the CLOCK OUT button is showing.

steps.title: Tap CLOCK OUT when you leave
steps.body: When your shift ends, tap this red CLOCK OUT button. That records your real hours to the minute. Do this every day — it is the only thing you have to remember, and it keeps your pay correct with nothing pending.
steps.narration: When your shift ends, tap the red CLOCK OUT button. That records your real hours to the minute and keeps your pay correct with nothing left pending.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the red CLOCK OUT button. Tap it and show the confirmation.

steps.title: If you forget: the 5-minute auto clock-out
steps.body: If you never clock out, the system closes your shift for you at your scheduled end time plus a 5-minute grace. Your scheduled hours are paid as normal — you are not left 'on the clock' overnight. It is marked as an automatic clock-out so it is clear it wasn't a manual punch.
steps.narration: If you forget entirely, the system clocks you out at your scheduled end plus five minutes, so you're never left on the clock overnight. Your scheduled hours are still paid.
steps.action_hint: Hold on the screen. Caption: auto clock-out at scheduled end + 5 minutes.

steps.title: Worked past your shift? The extra time needs approval
steps.body: If you actually work beyond your scheduled end plus the 5-minute grace, your scheduled time is paid right away — but the EXTRA minutes are held until your manager approves them. When you clock out late, the extra is sent to your manager automatically as a request; you don't file anything.
steps.narration: If you work past your shift plus the grace, your scheduled time is paid right away, but the extra minutes are held until your manager approves them. Clocking out late sends that request automatically.
steps.action_hint: Caption: extra time past shift = pending your manager's approval.

steps.title: Coming back for a second shift the same day
steps.body: If you were auto-clocked-out earlier and clock IN again later the same day, that second session is allowed — but it is held pending your manager's OK before it counts toward pay. A normal lunch break (where you clocked out yourself and came back) is not affected and needs no permission.
steps.narration: If you were auto-clocked-out earlier and clock in again later that day, the second session is held until your manager approves it. A normal lunch break you clocked out for yourself is unaffected.
steps.action_hint: Caption: second session after an auto clock-out = pending approval.

steps.title: How you'll know it's pending
steps.body: Whenever something is waiting on your manager, your clock screen shows a '⏳ Pending your manager's permission' note. You don't need to chase it — once your manager approves, that time is added to your hours automatically. If it is denied, that time is not paid, and you should speak to your manager.
steps.narration: Whenever something is waiting on your manager, your clock screen shows a pending note. Once they approve, the time is added automatically. If it's denied, that time isn't paid — talk to your manager.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the ⏳ pending banner on the kiosk if one is present.

tours.title: Approve late clock-outs & second sessions
tours.description: Reps are auto-clocked-out at their shift end + 5 minutes. Extra time worked, and a second session after that, wait here for your approval before they count toward pay.

steps.title: Where time-clock approvals live
steps.body: This is the Time-clock Permissions board, under Store Ops. Reps are automatically clocked out at their scheduled shift end plus a 5-minute grace. Two things then wait for your approval before they count toward pay: extra time worked past that cap, and a second session started after an auto clock-out. Click Next and we'll go through approving one.
steps.narration: This is the Time-clock Permissions board under Store Ops. Reps are auto-clocked-out at shift end plus five minutes. Extra time worked, and a second session after that, wait here for your approval.
steps.action_hint: Open /storeops/timeclock-permissions with at least one pending request.

steps.title: Your pending list
steps.body: Everything waiting on you is here, with the rep, store, date, what kind of request it is — extra time past shift, or a second session — and how many extra minutes are involved. The count next to the heading is how many are waiting.
steps.narration: Everything waiting on you is in this list: the rep, store, date, the kind of request, and how many extra minutes. The number by the heading is how many are pending.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the pending table and the count beside 'Permissions to approve'.

steps.title: Approving makes the time count
steps.body: Tap Approve and that held time is added to the rep's hours right away — the extra minutes are stamped onto the punch, or the second session starts counting. The tick IS the approval: it records that you approved it, and when. This is what the rep is waiting on.
steps.narration: Tap Approve and the held time counts immediately — the extra minutes are added, or the second session starts counting. The tick is the approval, recorded with your name and the time.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the green Approve button on a pending row and tap it.

steps.title: Denying leaves it uncounted
steps.body: If the extra time or second session shouldn't be paid, tap Deny. The rep keeps their scheduled hours, but the disputed time stays out of their pay. You can add a short reason so there's a record of why. Use this when someone clocked out late without a real reason.
steps.narration: If the time shouldn't be paid, tap Deny. The rep keeps their scheduled hours, but the disputed time stays out of pay. Add a short reason so there's a record.
steps.action_hint: Highlight the Deny button and show the reason prompt.

steps.title: The rep sees your decision
steps.body: Your decision shows on the rep's own clock screen — approved time appears in their hours, a denial clears the pending note. Decided requests move to the history below the pending list, so there's always a record of who approved what and when. Check this board at the end of each day so nobody's pay is left waiting.
steps.narration: Your decision shows on the rep's clock screen, and every decided request moves to the history below with who approved it and when. Check this board at the end of each day so no one's pay is left waiting.
steps.action_hint: Scroll to the decided/history section below the pending list.
